claim: A pure PWA on Android cannot perform continuous background GPS: navigator.geolocation.watchPosition stops when the page is backgrounded or the screen is off, the Geolocation API is not available in Service Workers, and Periodic Background Sync enforces a ~12h minimum interval and is not real-time.
explanation:
All three sub-claims are supported by primary sources, and together they establish that a pure PWA on Android cannot do continuous background GPS for a run-tracker.

(1) watchPosition stops when backgrounded/screen off on Android Chrome: CONFIRMED. The W3C Geolocation spec defines the interface as [Exposed=Window] only, so it is tied to a foreground document. Chromium issues 506435 / 41186218 ("Geolocation disabled when Chrome is in the background") and Chromium 585055 (Android WebView) document that on Android API 23+ Chrome/WebView stops delivering GPS fixes to watchPosition once not in the foreground, described as intended by-design behavior; Mozilla bugzilla 1482733 documents the same for Firefox on Android O+. Progressier's PWA capabilities reference states watchPosition "may stop reporting the user's location to your PWAs when the screen of the device is turned off." Minor nuance: some historical reports note a screen-ON backgrounded PWA may briefly continue with a persistent notification, but screen-off/suspension reliably halts it — consistent with the claim's "screen is off" framing.

(2) Geolocation API not available in Service Workers: CONFIRMED at spec level. The W3C Geolocation spec exposes Geolocation only to Window (partial interface Navigator { ... geolocation; }, [Exposed=Window]). W3C ServiceWorker issue #745 ("Expose GeoLocation to workers") has been open since 2015 and never shipped; Chromium issue 40810960 confirms it is unavailable in (extension) service workers because there is no navigator/document context. So a service worker cannot read GPS to keep tracking while the page is dead.

(3) Periodic Background Sync ~12h minimum and not real-time: CONFIRMED. The official Chrome explainer (quoted via the blink-dev Intent to Experiment thread and secondary writeups) states "Chrome ensures a gap of at least 12 hours (configurable through experiments) between periodicsync events." Current Chrome/MDN docs (2025) frame timing as browser-controlled based on site engagement and network, and explicitly recommend push notifications "for truly important updates," confirming it is not real-time and is unsuitable for a live run feed.

Net effect: there is no web-platform mechanism for a PWA to capture a continuous GPS track with the screen off / app backgrounded on Android, confirming a native wrapper (Capacitor/React Native/native) is required for that one feature.

claim: Transistor Software's background-geolocation SDK (both @transistorsoft/capacitor-background-geolocation and react-native-background-geolocation) is free in DEBUG builds and costs $399 USD one-time/perpetual for 1 app (Starter) for RELEASE Android builds, with the same pricing across Capacitor and React Native.
explanation:
Every component of the claim is supported by Transistor Software's own primary sources, checked 2026-06-01.

1) Free in DEBUG / paid for RELEASE Android: Both official GitHub READMEs state verbatim: "The SDK is fully functional in DEBUG builds — no license required. Try before you buy." and "A license is required only for RELEASE builds on Android." This was confirmed independently in BOTH the react-native-background-geolocation README and the capacitor-background-geolocation README.

2) $399 / 1 app / perpetual (Starter): The official pricing page docs.transistorsoft.com/purchase lists the Starter plan at $399 covering "1 application key" with a "Perpetual license" and "1 year access to latest updates." (Higher tiers: Venture $599/5 apps, Pro $749/25 apps, Studio $999/100 apps.) "Perpetual" license corresponds to the "one-time/perpetual" wording in the claim; note the price includes only 1 year of updates, after which the license still works perpetually but updates require renewal/upgrade.

3) Same pricing across Capacitor and React Native: The purchase page presents a single, unified pricing structure described as "identical pricing across React Native, Capacitor, Flutter, Cordova, and native frameworks," confirming parity between Capacitor and React Native.

No contradicting evidence was found. The only minor nuance worth flagging is that "perpetual" applies to the license key itself, while the $399 buys only 1 year of update access — but this does not contradict the one-time/perpetual characterization in the claim.

claim: The free MIT @capacitor-community/background-geolocation plugin throttles WebView HTTP requests after ~5 minutes in the background on Android (mitigated via a native HTTP plugin or android.useLegacyBridge=true), and requires POST_NOTIFICATIONS on Android 13+.
explanation: Every component of the claim is supported verbatim by the plugin's official README (master branch) and confirmed against the npm registry. (1) License + cost: package.json and the npm registry both list license "MIT"; it is a free, open-source community plugin. (2) Throttling: the README states verbatim "If your app forwards location updates to a server in real time, be aware that after 5 minutes in the background Android will throttle HTTP requests initiated from the WebView." (3) Mitigations: the README gives BOTH mitigations cited in the claim -- "The solution is to use a native HTTP plugin such as [CapacitorHttp]" AND "Set the `android.useLegacyBridge` option to `true` in your Capacitor configuration. This prevents location updates halting after 5 minutes in the background." (4) Android 13+: the README states "On Android 13+, the app needs the `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` runtime permission to show the persistent notification informing the user that their location is being used in the background." One minor nuance to flag for precision (does not change the verdict): the throttling described is of WebView-initiated HTTP requests (the data-sync failure mode the claim warns about); useLegacyBridge is documented specifically as preventing *location updates* from halting after 5 minutes, while CapacitorHttp/native HTTP is the documented fix for the *HTTP-request* throttling. Both are listed in the README as the claim states, so the claim's framing of them as mitigations is accurate. Current version at time of check: 1.2.26, published 2025-08-28 (registry last modified 2026-01-29). Evidence is version- and time-sensitive: README wording, the 5-minute behavior, and the Android 13+ permission requirement reflect this version and current Android behavior, and could change in future plugin releases or Android OS versions.

claim: Any app requesting ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION must pass Google Play's background-location permission declaration review (prominent disclosure + demo video showing disclosure, runtime prompt, and the background feature) regardless of whether it is built with Capacitor, React Native/Expo, or native Kotlin.
explanation:
Primary sources confirm both parts of the claim.

REVIEW GATE EXISTS: Google's official Play Console Help page "Understanding location in the background permissions" (support.google.com/.../answer/9799150) states that if an app's AAB/APK targets Android 10 (API 29) or higher and includes the ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION permission in its manifest, the developer MUST complete the Permissions Declaration Form (App content > Sensitive app permissions > Location permissions) and obtain approval. The same page requires: (a) an in-app PROMINENT DISCLOSURE shown during normal app use (not buried in settings/menu or privacy policy) before the location runtime permission prompt, describing what data is accessed/collected and how it is used/shared; and (b) a DEMO VIDEO (recommended <=30s, YouTube or MP4 link) that shows the declared background-location feature in action, the steps to reach/enable it, the prominent disclosure dialog, and the device runtime permission with user consent. This matches the claim's three required video elements (disclosure, runtime prompt, background feature). The feature must be core to the app's main purpose; "nice to have" background tracking is rejected.

FRAMEWORK-AGNOSTIC: This is sound by mechanism rather than by an explicit per-framework statement from Google. The Play review gate is triggered purely by the presence of ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION in the uploaded app's Android manifest (Android Developers docs confirm it is a manifest-level <uses-permission> declaration). Capacitor, React Native/Expo, and native Kotlin all produce a standard Android AAB/APK whose manifest declares this same permission, and Play's review operates on that uploaded artifact, not on the build toolchain. No primary source describes any exemption based on how the app is built, so a run-tracker doing background GPS will hit this gate under any of these approaches. The only way to avoid it is to not request ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION at all (e.g., foreground-only tracking with a persistent foreground service while the app/feature is active), which changes the product behavior.

TIME-SENSITIVE FLAG (April 2026 policy): Google announced Play policy updates on April 15, 2026 (support.google.com/.../answer/16926792) with at least a 30-day compliance window. These TIGHTEN location handling -- introducing the location button as the recommended minimum scope for precise location, removing geofencing as an approved foreground-services use case (requiring migration to the Geofence API), and reinforcing that background/always-on location must be justified as core functionality via the developer declaration process. They do NOT remove the declaration/prominent-disclosure/demo-video review requirement; if anything they raise the justification bar. So the underlying claim remains true post-April-2026, but exact wording and adjacent foreground-service rules are evolving and should be re-checked against the live policy pages before release.

claim: OpenFreeMap's public instance currently has NO enforced limit on map views/requests and allows commercial use (donation-funded; a per-referer soft cap is only a future plan).
explanation:
All four sub-claims are supported by OpenFreeMap's own primary sources.

1) NO enforced limit (current): The official homepage FAQ (openfreemap.org) states verbatim: "Using our public instance is completely free: there are no limits on the number of map views or requests." It also confirms "no registration, no user database, no API keys, and no cookies." The same wording appears in the GitHub README (hyperknot/openfreemap). This is framed as the current reality, with no conditional language.

2) Commercial use allowed: The homepage FAQ explicitly answers "Is commercial usage allowed? Yes." (Note: the separate Terms of Service page, last updated Feb 26, 2025, is minimal and does NOT itself restrict commercial use — it only prohibits illegal use, service disruption, IP violation, and unauthorized automated data collection. So nothing contradicts the "Yes" on the FAQ.)

3) Donation-funded: The homepage states the project aims to "cover the running costs of our public instance through donations" (GitHub Sponsors / support plans, no mandatory payment). The author's blog post (Zsolt Ero, "OpenFreeMap survived 100,000 requests per second," dated Aug 9, 2025) confirms: "the project currently runs on $500/month in donations. This is just enough to cover all infrastructure costs."

4) Per-referer cap is only a future PLAN, not enforced: The Aug 9, 2025 blog post frames it as planned/not-yet-implemented: "I need to implement bandwidth limiting by referer" with "a very high number, like 100 million requests per 24 hours or something similar," and for native apps "I'll probably ask them to add a custom header." OpenFreeMap's own description elsewhere uses future tense ("everything will still stay free... but every referer will be limited to a very high number"). No source indicates this cap is currently active.

I attempted to refute the claim by checking the standalone ToS and searching for 2026 pricing/term changes; I found no hard cap, no commercial restriction, and no evidence the per-referer cap has been activated. The claim stands as confirmed.

CAVEAT / FRAGILITY for the PoC (the reason this matters): OpenFreeMap is a single-operator, donation-funded service ($500/month) explicitly provided "as-is" with the operator's right to "discontinue it at any time without notice" (ToS). The planned ~100M req/24h per-referer cap is generous for a PoC but is provider-discretion and not contractually guaranteed; native apps may later need a custom identifying header. The author has stated intent to add per-referer limiting "soon" (as of Aug 2025), so the "no enforced limit" status is genuinely time-sensitive. Recommendation aligns with the prompt: keep the Protomaps self-host path (PMTiles + own style) ready as a fallback. Note that even if the ~100M/day cap activates, it would still be a high soft cap, not a commercial-use ban.

claim: MapTiler free = 100,000 requests/mo + 5,000 sessions/mo + 100 MB hosting (pauses when exhausted); Stadia Maps free = 2,500 credits/mo and is non-commercial/eval only.
explanation:
The MapTiler half of the claim is fully CONFIRMED by the official pricing page (https://www.maptiler.com/cloud/pricing/, fetched twice). The free "Basic" plan lists exactly: 100,000 (100 thousand) API requests/month, 5,000 (5 thousand) API sessions/month, and 100 MB of hosting. The page explicitly states "On a FREE plan service will pause until the next month" — confirming the pause-when-exhausted behavior (paid plans instead incur overage charges). The page also confirms the free plan is for "personal / non-commercial use," with commercial use starting at the Flex tier ($25/mo).

The Stadia Maps half is MIXED. The non-commercial/evaluation-only characterization is CONFIRMED: the docs (https://docs.stadiamaps.com/limits/) state "Our free tier is available for development, evaluation, and non-commercial use (including academic use)," and the FAQ states "Use of Stadia Maps' services commercially requires a paid subscription or (in some cases) a custom license." HOWEVER, the credit figure is REFUTED. The official pricing page (https://stadiamaps.com/pricing/, fetched twice) consistently shows the Free plan includes 200,000 credits/month with no additional usage allowed — NOT 2,500. (For comparison the page lists Starter = 1,000,000, Standard = 7,500,000, Professional = 25,000,000 credits/month.) The "2,500 credits/mo" number appears only in a third-party blog (skywork.ai), never on any Stadia primary source; it is wrong by roughly 80x.

IMPORTANT NUANCE / CLAIMS TO VERIFY: (1) Stadia bills in "credits," not "requests" — different API calls cost different credit amounts (a map tile costs far less than a geocoding/routing/matrix call, per Stadia's credit schedule), so 200,000 credits is NOT directly comparable to a flat request count and yields far more than 200,000 tile loads in practice. (2) When Stadia free credits are exhausted, APIs return HTTP 429 Rate Limit Exceeded (per docs), and the account is emailed at 80% usage. (3) All free-tier figures are time-sensitive: MapTiler's 100k/5k/100MB and Stadia's 200k credits + non-commercial clause should be re-checked against the live pricing pages before any cost/legal decision, as both vendors have changed credit schedules historically (e.g., Stadia's 2023 and Fall 2024 credit updates). (4) For a live GPS app, the binding legal point is that BOTH MapTiler's free Basic tier AND Stadia Maps' free tier prohibit commercial use — a managed free tier is only viable for the PoC/eval phase, not a launched commercial product.

claim: On-device/native PMTiles is supported as of MapLibre Native Android 11.8.0 / iOS 6.10.0 (and thus the matching @maplibre/maplibre-react-native v11.x), enabling offline self-hosted tiles in RN/Capacitor.
explanation:
Primary sources confirm the exact version numbers. The MapLibre Native raw CHANGELOG (fetched via GitHub API, file at platform/android/CHANGELOG.md) lists under header "## 11.8.0": "Add PMTiles support (#2882)". The iOS CHANGELOG (platform/ios/CHANGELOG.md) lists under header "## 6.10.0": "Add support for PMTiles with pmtiles:// URL scheme (#2882)" -- the same PR #2882 landed in both platforms. The official MapLibre January 2025 newsletter independently states "MapLibre Android 11.8.0 and MapLibre iOS 6.10.0 were released which included the new PMTiles support for MapLibre Native." So the native SDK versions in the claim are correct.

The second part -- that maplibre-react-native v11.x carries PMTiles-capable native SDKs -- also holds. The v11.0.0 release (published 2026-04-17, GitHub API) bundles Android MapLibre Native 13.0.2 and iOS 6.25.0 as its final pinned versions (with intermediate bumps recorded through Android 11.10.1 / 12.2.3 and iOS 6.14.0 / 6.22.1). Every one of these is at or above the 11.8.0 / 6.10.0 PMTiles threshold, so any v11.x release includes native PMTiles support. PMTiles is loaded via the pmtiles:// URL prefix (https:// for remote, asset:// for bundled assets, file:// for local files) -- the file:// and asset:// schemes are what enable genuinely offline self-hosted tiles, supporting the "offline self-hosted tiles" portion of the claim.

CAVEATS / things to verify against your pinned version: (1) Minor doc inconsistency -- the MapLibre Android PMTiles *example* page states "Starting MapLibre Android 11.7.0, using PMTiles as a data source is supported," which conflicts with the CHANGELOG/newsletter (11.8.0). The 11.8.0/6.10.0 numbers in the claim match the authoritative CHANGELOG and newsletter; the "11.7.0" appears to be a documentation error. Either way, any 11.8.0+ build (and all v11.x RN releases) include it. (2) IMPORTANT limitation, time/version-sensitive: PMTiles sources currently do NOT support offline pack downloads or the SDK tile cache (per MapLibre docs). "Offline" works in the sense of loading a local file:// or asset:// PMTiles archive, but you cannot use MapLibre's OfflineManager/offline-pack mechanism with a PMTiles source. For the project's offline-map goal, bundling/sideloading a .pmtiles file is the supported path, not offline-pack caching. (3) The claim mentions Capacitor: native PMTiles in MapLibre *Native* applies to RN; in Capacitor you would typically use MapLibre GL JS (web/WebGL), where PMTiles is handled via the protomaps pmtiles.js addProtocol -- a different (also viable) mechanism, not the MapLibre Native code path verified here. (4) Verify the actual native SDK version your specific pinned maplibre-react-native v11.x release resolves to (it is configurable and the bundled default has moved well past 11.8.0/6.10.0).

claim: Terra Draw (@watergis/maplibre-gl-terradraw) and route-snapper are web/JS only with no React Native build, while mapbox-gl-draw is effectively unmaintained for MapLibre.
explanation:
The two "web/JS only" sub-claims are CONFIRMED by primary sources; the "mapbox-gl-draw is effectively unmaintained" sub-claim is REFUTED as worded. Hence partly-true.

(1) TERRA DRAW = WEB-ONLY: CONFIRMED. terra-draw's GitHub README and npm package (v1.31.0, published 2026-05-29) list exactly six adapters, ALL of which are browser DOM/canvas mapping libraries: Leaflet, OpenLayers, MapLibre GL JS, Google Maps JS API, Mapbox GL JS, ArcGIS JS SDK. The package ships only browser entry points (main: ./dist/terra-draw.cjs, module: ./dist/terra-draw.module.js) with no "react-native" field. The @watergis/maplibre-gl-terradraw wrapper (v1.13.2, published 2026-05-30) hard-depends on maplibre-gl ^4.0.0||^5.0.0 — i.e., the WebGL JS engine, which is NOT the same as maplibre-react-native (a separate project that wraps MapLibre Native for Android/iOS). Neither library mentions or supports React Native. So Terra Draw drawing forces a WebView in an RN/Capacitor/PWA context.

(2) ROUTE-SNAPPER = WEB-ONLY: CONFIRMED. route_snapper (dabreegster) is Rust compiled to WASM that runs in the browser with a thin JS wrapper; integration constructs a RouteSnapper from a graph file plus a MapLibre GL JS map instance. The npm package route-snapper (v0.4.9, published 2024-11-25) exposes only route_snapper.js with no react-native entry point and no mention of RN. Web/WASM-in-browser only.

(3) MAPBOX-GL-DRAW "EFFECTIVELY UNMAINTAINED FOR MAPLIBRE": REFUTED as stated; the accurate nuance differs. (a) Maintenance: @mapbox/mapbox-gl-draw is NOT unmaintained — the latest release is v1.5.1 published 2025-11-03 (registry time.modified 2025-11-03T14:12:48Z), following v1.5.0 on 2024-12-04. Activity is low/sporadic but the project received a release within the last ~7 months. (b) MapLibre fit: it is genuinely NOT built for MapLibre — it targets mapbox-gl-js and only works with MapLibre via a manual hack (reassigning MapboxDraw.constants.classes to maplibregl-* CSS classes), as shown in MapLibre's own official example for v1.5.0; broke outright with MapLibre 3.x. So the correct framing is "not natively MapLibre-targeted, works only via a CSS-class workaround, and low-activity," NOT "effectively unmaintained."

VERSION/TIME SENSITIVITY (flag for re-check): terra-draw 1.31.0 (2026-05-29), @watergis/maplibre-gl-terradraw 1.13.2 (2026-05-30), route-snapper 0.4.9 (2024-11-25, stale ~18mo — could be abandoned or revived), @mapbox/mapbox-gl-draw 1.5.1 (2025-11-03). RN-support and maintenance status of all four can change; re-verify npm publish dates and the adapters list before committing. Note also that Maplibre-Geoman is positioned as the actively-maintained commercial alternative for MapLibre web drawing in 2025-2026, but it is likewise web-JS only.

claim: OpenRouteService free hosted tier currently allows ~2,000 directions requests/day with a sliding 40 requests/minute limit (and round_trip max ~100 km).
explanation:
All three numbers in the claim are supported by current ORS primary documentation.

1) Daily quota (~2,000/day) and 2) per-minute limit (sliding 40/min): The official ORS backend documentation FAQ (giscience.github.io/openrouteservice, the maintained current docs) states verbatim that "the directions endpoint and its default limit of 2000 requests per day" and that "The minutely limit is enforced as a sliding window, meaning that any consecutive period of 60 seconds may only contain 40 directions requests." It also documents the enforcement behavior: 403 Forbidden on the daily limit and 429 Too Many Requests on the minutely limit, with x-ratelimit-remaining / x-ratelimit-reset headers. This exactly matches the "2,000/day" and "sliding 40 requests/minute" parts of the claim.

3) round_trip ~100 km: The official restrictions page (openrouteservice.org/restrictions) confirms that "Alternative & round trip routes" have a maximum distance of 100 km, matching the claim's "round_trip max ~100 km."

Corroboration on currency/JWT migration: Searches confirm the user-management migration to account.heigit.org in early 2025 and that newly issued keys look like JWTs (eyJ... prefix) but function as regular HeiGIT API keys. An August 25, 2025 forum thread on ask.openrouteservice.org ("Rate limitation do not match current plan") shows a user being capped at 40 directions requests/minute (a HeiGIT rep confirmed limits differ per endpoint), which is consistent with 40/min remaining the directions default after the migration. No evidence was found that the 2025-2026 JWT migration revised these directions numbers.

CAVEATS / things to verify on your own account:
- The FAQ frames 2,000/day as the "default" directions limit rather than as a hard, plan-specific guarantee. The literal Standard (free) plan figure lives on account.heigit.org/info/plans, which is a JavaScript-rendered single-page app I could NOT scrape (it returned only "HeiGIT Account" with no figures). So the exact free-plan daily number shown in your dashboard post-login should be confirmed directly there — the "~2,000" is from documentation, not from a rendered plans table.
- These are quotas/limits that HeiGIT can change at any time (they have historically adjusted them, e.g., COVID-era increases). Treat them as time-sensitive.
- The 40/min applies to directions specifically; other endpoints (matrix, isochrones, optimization, geocoding) have different per-minute and daily limits, so do not assume 40/min globally.
- Practical PoC note: 2,000 directions/day with a 40/min ceiling is fine for hand-drawn snap-to-road and occasional AI loop generation, but live tracking should NOT call directions repeatedly per-tick; the cap is per-key, so heavy/bursty AI route generation can hit the 40/min sliding window quickly. The directions standard-profile max distance is 6,000 km, but round_trip (loop-by-distance) is capped at 100 km.

claim: Mapbox Map Matching, Directions, and Isochrone each have a ~100,000 requests/month free tier (Map Matching/Isochrone capped at 300 req/min), billed ~$2.00/1k above that. (Plus a "Why it matters" note that a billing account/credit card is required even within the free tier.)
explanation:
The core pricing claim is confirmed by Mapbox primary sources (verified 2026-06-01).

FREE TIER (100,000/month): mapbox.com/pricing lists ALL THREE APIs -- Directions, Map Matching, and Isochrone -- with a free tier of "Up to 100,000" monthly requests. Confirmed exactly as stated.

PRICE ABOVE FREE TIER (~$2.00/1k): Confirmed. For all three APIs the first paid tier (100,001-500,000 requests) is $2.00 per 1,000. Note this is tiered, so it DECREASES at higher volume: $1.60/1k at 500,001-1,000,000, $1.20/1k at 1,000,001+, and contact-sales discounts at 5,000,000+. So "~$2.00/1k above that" is accurate as the entry rate but is a ceiling, not a flat rate.

RATE LIMITS (300 req/min): Confirmed. The Map Matching API docs state verbatim "The Map Matching API is limited to 300 requests per minute." The Isochrone API docs state verbatim "The Isochrone API is limited to 300 requests per minute." (The claim correctly scopes the 300 req/min cap to only Map Matching and Isochrone; the Directions API docs do not state a 300 req/min limit -- it has different, higher per-mode limits not at issue here.)

CREDIT CARD / BILLING ACCOUNT REQUIRED (from the "Why it matters" note): This is the one nuance and is only PARTLY supported. Mapbox's "How does Pay-as-you-go billing work?" FAQ says a card is RECOMMENDED ("we do recommend adding a credit card... especially if you're using Mapbox in production"), not strictly mandated for free-tier-only use. Other Mapbox account/invoice docs say a valid card is needed to verify account ownership and avoid deactivation. So "a credit card is required even within the free tier" is closer to strongly-recommended/needed-for-account-verification than an absolute hard gate on every free-tier request. The pricing/rate-limit substance of the claim -- the part that determines viability -- is fully confirmed.

TIME/VERSION SENSITIVITY: Mapbox revises pricing periodically. Figures verified against the live mapbox.com/pricing page and current API docs as of 2026-06-01. Re-confirm before depending on it.

claim: GraphHopper's algorithm=round_trip works with the foot/hike profile and requires ch.disable=true (flexible/hybrid mode), preventing use of Contraction Hierarchies speed-up for that profile.
explanation:
Confirmed by GraphHopper's own primary sources (master branch, checked 2026-06-01), at both documentation and source-code level.

(1) round_trip requires ch.disable=true / flexible mode. The official api-doc.md lists the `algorithm` parameter (with options dijkstra, astar, astarbi, alternative_route, round_trip) under the "### Flexible" section, prefaced by: "Unlock certain flexible features via `ch.disable=true` per request or disable CH on the server-side by using an empty list for `profiles_ch`. The only exception is the parameter `algorithm=alternative_route` which is also available without specifying `ch.disable=true`." Since alternative_route is named as the ONLY exception, round_trip is a flexible-only feature requiring ch.disable=true (or no CH for that profile). This is enforced in source: CHRoutingAlgorithmFactory.java only accepts ASTAR_BI, DIJKSTRA_BI, and ALT_ROUTE, and throws IllegalArgumentException ("Algorithm ... not supported for node-based/edge-based Contraction Hierarchies. Try with ch.disable=true") for anything else, including round_trip. So a round_trip query genuinely cannot run in CH/speed mode.

(2) round_trip works with the foot profile. There is no profile-type restriction on round_trip in the docs or schema; it is a valid algorithm for any flexible profile. config-example.yml ships a `foot` profile (custom_model_files: foot.json, foot_elevation.json). round_trip behavior is generic across profiles (a forum thread confirmed a working round_trip response, though there with bike). The hike profile likewise exists as an in-built custom model (hike.json). So foot/hike + round_trip is supported.

(3) "Preventing use of CH speed-up for that profile" — accurate, with an important nuance. round_trip queries themselves cannot use CH; they always run in flexible (or hybrid/LM) mode, raising per-query CPU/RAM. Note that by DEFAULT the foot profile is not CH-prepared anyway: config-example.yml states "By default foot and bike are without CH preparation as this requires less resources. Add them to 'profiles_ch' if you need it," and the default profiles_ch contains only `car`. So on a default config, foot has no CH speed-up regardless. The practical implication for config.yml on the constrained Oracle VM: you can still keep `foot` in profiles_ch to get CH speed-up for ordinary A-to-B foot routing, but any round_trip request must pass ch.disable=true (which requires CH to be disabling-allowed server-side, e.g. via hybrid/LM preparation or omitting foot from profiles_ch) and will be slower/heavier than a CH query. Equally, you can simply leave foot out of profiles_ch (the default) so round_trip foot requests work without needing the disabling flag.

Caveats: evidence is from the master branch on 2026-06-01; the api-doc "only exception is alternative_route" wording and the CHRoutingAlgorithmFactory supported-algorithm set are version-sensitive. round_trip quality/behavior for the foot profile (it injects randomness and uses a heading/seed) should still be empirically validated on the self-hosted build before committing, as the claim's "why it matters" note urges.

claim: A single-country OSM extract (e.g. Germany ~300 MB PBF) runs GraphHopper in ~4-8 GB RAM and Valhalla in ~8-16 GB, both fitting on the Oracle Ampere A1 always-free VM (4 OCPU / 24 GB RAM / 200 GB block storage).
explanation:
The central conclusion holds: both GraphHopper and Valhalla can run a single-country (Germany) extract within the Oracle Ampere A1 always-free VM, and that VM's specs are stated correctly. Oracle's official docs confirm the free A1.Flex shape gives up to 4 OCPU / 24 GB RAM / 200 GB block storage. Disk is a non-issue: a Germany GraphHopper graph is single-digit GB and Valhalla's Germany tiles are ~4.6 GB. BUT several premises are wrong or misleading:

1) PBF SIZE IS WRONG (~10-15x off). The claim says Germany is "~300 MB PBF." It is not. GraphHopper's own June 2022 hosting blog lists Germany at 3.6 GB PBF (~24.3M edges), and the canonical Geofabrik germany-latest.osm.pbf is currently 4.4 GB (data up to 2026-05-31). 300 MB is roughly a single German state, not the whole country. This matters because both engines' RAM/disk needs scale with PBF size.

2) GRAPHHOPPER "~4-8 GB" CONFLATES QUERY vs IMPORT. GraphHopper's documented rule of thumb is ~1-1.5x (blog says ~2x for one profile) the PBF size for the graph, and the on-disk graph roughly equals its in-RAM footprint. Against the REAL 4.4 GB PBF, a single foot/CH profile query server lands roughly in the 4-8 GB band, so the figure is coincidentally plausible for serving routes. However, GraphHopper docs explicitly state import needs more RAM than serving, and CH/turn-cost preparation pushes import RAM higher; with the true PBF size the 4-8 GB band is tight for import. The claim's reasoning only works because the actual PBF is ~10x bigger than stated.

3) VALHALLA "~8-16 GB" IS OVERSTATED FOR TYPICAL ROUTING. Valhalla is tile-based with a low default 1 GB cache. A July 2024 maintainer-involved discussion on Germany data shows idle/baseline tile memory of ~1.2-1.5 GB and ~4-6 GB total at idle; the 8-16 GB figures only appear under heavy 200-400-location matrix requests and multi-threaded operation (memory grows linearly with server_threads). For plain foot/pedestrian A-to-B routing, Germany Valhalla uses well under 8 GB. So the band describes a worst case, not normal routing.

Net: the headline ("both fit on one 24 GB free VM alongside Postgres + Caddy") is CONFIRMED for a single country, but the supporting numbers are sloppy — the 300 MB Germany figure is flatly wrong, GraphHopper's band mixes query vs import, and Valhalla's band is high for typical use. The claim's own caveat (larger regions like Europe/continents blow past the free tier) is correct: GraphHopper Europe is a 25 GB PBF / ~40-60 GB RAM and full planet needs 60-120 GB, far beyond 24 GB.

claim: As of terms effective 2026-03-23, Google uses FREE/unpaid-tier Gemini API prompts and responses to improve/train its products, and human reviewers may read them; paid tier does not.
explanation:
The official Google Gemini API Additional Terms of Service (ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms), with an effective date of March 23, 2026, confirm every element of the claim. UNPAID SERVICES (Google AI Studio + free/unpaid quota of the Gemini API): under the section "How Google Uses Your Data," the terms state "Google uses the content you submit to the Services and any generated responses to provide, improve, and develop Google products and services," and "human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output." PAID SERVICES (paid quota of the Gemini API): the terms state "Google doesn't use your prompts (including associated system instructions, cached content, and files such as images, videos, or documents) or responses to improve our products"; for paid usage, data is processed under the Data Processing Addendum and retained only to detect/prevent Prohibited Use Policy violations and for legal compliance.

IMPORTANT PRACTICAL NUANCE for the "why it matters" PII question: even on the unpaid tier, the terms say Google discloses that it disconnects the data "from your Google Account, API key, and Cloud project before reviewers see or annotate it." Critically, Google ALSO explicitly instructs: "Do not submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information to the Unpaid Services." So the free tier is unsafe for user PII (names, home start coordinates) on two grounds: (1) it is used to train Google products and (2) Google itself prohibits submitting personal information there. The correct mitigations remain: anonymize/strip PII before sending, or use the paid tier (or a self-hosted model) for any personalized request. Note the disconnection step is a de-identification effort, not a guarantee against re-identification, and "anonymized" location/start-point data can still be sensitive.

TIME/VERSION-SENSITIVE: Terms version effective 2026-03-23 (verified today, 2026-06-01). Google revises these Additional Terms periodically (prior known versions include 2024-05, 2024-12-20, and a 2025 version); the unpaid-vs-paid data-use distinction has been consistent across recent versions, but the exact wording, the human-reviewer disclosure, and any free-tier scope should be re-checked before relying on them in production, as Google may revise without breaking the URL.

claim: Groq free tier: Llama 3.1 8B allows ~14,400 requests/day (500k tokens/day) while most other models are 1,000 RPD / 6,000 TPM / 30 RPM, no credit card required.
explanation:
The load-bearing numbers are CONFIRMED by Groq's official rate-limits documentation (console.groq.com/docs/rate-limits, fetched 2026-06-01): llama-3.1-8b-instant on the Free plan = 30 RPM, 14,400 RPD, 6,000 TPM, 500,000 TPD. By contrast llama-3.3-70b-versatile = 30 RPM, 1,000 RPD (1K), 12,000 TPM, 100,000 TPD. So the central thesis -- the 8B model's far higher daily request/token allowance (14,400 RPD / 500k TPD vs ~1,000 RPD for the typical model) -- holds, and this remains a valid basis for picking 8B as the primary $0 provider. No credit card is required: signup at console.groq.com via email/Google/GitHub gives immediate API access (confirmed by multiple 2026 sources). 

The claim is only PARTLY true on the secondary descriptors of 'most other models': (1) The '6,000 TPM' figure is NOT representative -- the official table shows llama-3.3-70b-versatile at 12,000 TPM, and TPM ranges roughly 6,000-12,000+ across models (some models also get 60 RPM, e.g. qwen3-32b/kimi-k2). So '6,000 TPM / 30 RPM' is not a universal 'other models' baseline. (2) Note the 8B model itself ALSO has 30 RPM and 6,000 TPM -- identical to the baseline -- so its advantage is purely on the DAILY caps (RPD and TPD), not on the per-minute limits. The claim's framing slightly implies the 8B differs on TPM/RPM too, which it does not. (3) '1,000 RPD for most other models' is broadly correct for the headline chat models but not literally all (whisper-large-v3 = 2K RPD, groq/compound = 250 RPD, llama-4-maverick = 500 RPD). 

Bottom line: the recommendation's quantitative foundation is sound and unchanged as of June 2026; only the imprecise '6,000 TPM' generalization and the implication that 8B beats others on per-minute limits are inaccurate.

claim: An 8B model at Q4_K_M needs ~6 GB RAM and runs at single-digit tok/s CPU-only, and the Oracle Cloud free-tier VM (Ampere A1, up to 24 GB) is CPU-only — making self-hosted Ollama viable but slow for interactive suggestions.
explanation:
All four sub-claims hold up against primary and corroborating sources, though one figure (tok/s) sits at the edge of "single-digit" and rests mostly on secondary estimates rather than a primary 4-OCPU benchmark.

1) ~6 GB RAM for 8B Q4_K_M — CONFIRMED. The llama.cpp GitHub discussion #8793 reports the Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M file at exactly 4,920,738,944 bytes (~4.58 GiB / ~5 GB on disk). Adding KV cache (~256 MB at 4K) and runtime overhead brings practical RAM use to ~6-7 GB at modest context (community RAM tables cite 6-7 GB for any 8B Q4_K_M). NOTE: with llama.cpp's default 128k context it can balloon to ~16 GB, so "~6 GB" assumes a sane context window (8K) — which Ollama defaults to. The figure is accurate for typical use.

2) Single-digit tok/s CPU-only — SUPPORTED but borderline. The relevant hardware is the free-tier 4-OCPU instance. Multiple guides put a 7B/8B Q4_K_M at ~5-8 tok/s on 4 OCPU (one 2026 guide says ~8-12 tok/s for 7B). So it is genuinely slow and largely single-digit, but estimates can edge slightly into low double digits depending on threads/context/quant. CAUTION on a common confound: Ampere/Oracle's headline "up to 91 tok/s" for Llama 3 8B (Oracle AI blog, May 29 2024) and Ampere's "85.6 tok/s" were measured on 64-80 OCPU instances with Ampere-optimized llama.cpp — NOT the 4-OCPU free tier. Do not cite those for the free VM.

3) Oracle free-tier Ampere A1, up to 24 GB, CPU-only — CONFIRMED by primary source. Oracle's official Always Free docs specify the VM.Standard.A1.Flex allowance as 4 OCPUs and 24 GB memory total (3,000 OCPU-hours + 18,000 GB-hours/month), allocatable across up to 4 instances. The docs offer no GPU in the Always Free tier; a 2026 guide confirms "no GPUs in the free tier; GPU shapes require a paid account." So it is CPU-only (Arm/Ampere).

4) "Viable but slow for interactive suggestions" — SUPPORTED. Sources explicitly describe this throughput as "suitable for non-latency-sensitive tasks but not ideal for interactive use cases that require faster responses." For your project this means self-hosted Ollama is realistic as an async/background route-suggestion path, but RAM contention is real: 8B Q4_K_M (~6-7 GB) plus Postgres plus a routing engine on a 24 GB VM is feasible but leaves limited headroom, and interactive (sub-second) LLM latency is not achievable. A smaller model (3B/4B) or a managed free-tier LLM API would better serve interactive natural-language suggestions.

claim: Firebase Realtime Database Spark (free) tier = 100 simultaneous connections, 1 GB stored, 10 GB/month download (as of 2025-2026). Firestore Spark = 1 GB stored + per-DAY 50k reads / 20k writes / 20k deletes.
explanation:
Every number in the claim is verified against Google's own primary sources (fetched 2026-06-01).

REALTIME DATABASE (Spark) — confirmed on the official Firebase pricing page (firebase.google.com/pricing): Simultaneous connections = 100; Stored = 1 GB; Downloaded = 10 GB/month. The 100-connection cap is independently corroborated by the official RTDB limits doc (firebase.google.com/docs/database/usage/limits), which states "The Spark plan limit on simultaneous connections is 100" (vs. 200,000 on paid plans). Note the doc's definition: one "simultaneous connection" = one mobile device, browser tab, OR server app connected at a given time — directly relevant to the live multi-runner tracking use case, since each runner's open app/tab consumes one of the 100 slots.

CLOUD FIRESTORE (Spark) — confirmed on the same pricing page: Stored data = 1 GiB total (page shows "GiB"; the claim says "1 GB" — effectively equivalent at this granularity, GiB is the precise unit); Document reads = 50K/day; Document writes = 20K/day; Document deletes = 20K/day. These are per-day quotas as the claim states.

Minor precision note: Firestore storage is listed as 1 GiB (binary, ~1.074 GB) rather than 1 GB (decimal) on the official page, but this does not materially change the claim. All other figures match exactly.

For the PoC's hard ceilings: the 100-connection RTDB cap means at most ~100 concurrent live-tracking clients before connections are refused; Firestore's 20k writes/day is the binding constraint for write-heavy live GPS streaming (e.g., a single runner writing position once/sec for ~5.5 hours would alone exhaust the daily write quota), making RTDB generally the better-fit free option for high-frequency location updates.

claim: A pure PWA on Android cannot maintain a WebSocket/realtime connection or continuous GPS emission once the screen is off or the app is backgrounded; an Android foreground service (reachable only via Capacitor/React Native/native, not PWA) is required for background live tracking.
explanation:
Primary and corroborating sources converge on every load-bearing part of this claim, with only a minor wording nuance on the WebSocket point.

(1) PWA background GPS does NOT work. The Web Geolocation API is exposed only via navigator.geolocation on the Window context; it is NOT available in Service Workers (W3C ServiceWorker issue #745 requests adding it, confirming its absence). Geolocation watchPosition() stops emitting once the page is backgrounded or the screen is off on Android 8 (Oreo) and above. Mozilla bug #1482733 (open/NEW since 2018, marked wontfix for FF 63-65) documents exactly this: "GPS updates now immediately stop in firefox after the phone's display is powered off," with the stated root cause being Android O background limits that block location unless the app shows a foreground notification. A user reports their GPS-recording web app "has become useless ... now that I switched to Android 10." Android's own docs confirm the OS computes a new background location only "a few times each hour" without a foreground service.

(2) PWA realtime/WebSocket does NOT survive backgrounding/screen-off. The Page Lifecycle API (Chrome 68+) formalizes system-initiated FROZEN and DISCARDED states; a standalone PWA/Chrome tab on Android "will freeze at one point when in the background" and "tabs are commonly discarded after a few minutes backgrounded when Chrome evicts the renderer." During the freeze callback, "network activity will be disallowed (except fetch keep-alive)," and a discarded page tears down the renderer entirely — killing any WebSocket. (Nuance/precision flag: Chrome 57+ does exempt tabs with active WebSocket/WebRTC connections from background TIMER throttling, so a foregrounded-but-inactive tab may hold a socket; but this exemption does NOT prevent the OS-level freeze/discard once the PWA is truly backgrounded or the screen is off, so the practical claim holds.)

(3) An Android foreground service IS the required mechanism, and it is reachable only via native code. Android docs state foreground services "show a status bar notification" and explicitly list "A fitness app that records a user's run in a foreground service" as the canonical use case. On Android 14+, an app using location MUST declare android:foregroundServiceType="location", hold the FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION permission, and (to start it while backgrounded) hold ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION. A persistent, non-hideable notification is OS-mandated. The web platform exposes NO API to start an Android foreground service; GoogleChrome/android-browser-helper issue #496 confirms the only PWA path is to wrap the PWA in a TWA and implement background geolocation in NATIVE Android code, passing coordinates to JS via postMessage — i.e., the foreground service lives in native code, exactly as the claim states for Capacitor/React Native/native.

Net: A pure PWA cannot deliver continuous background GPS or a persistent realtime connection with the screen off/app backgrounded on Android; a native foreground service (via Capacitor, React Native, or a TWA native wrapper) is required. Confirmed.

claim: Supabase Realtime free tier = 200 concurrent peak connections + 2,000,000 messages/month (256 KB max), and free projects pause after ~1 week of inactivity; self-host connection limit is configurable via max_concurrent_users.
explanation:
Every component is confirmed by primary Supabase sources as of 2026-06-01.

1) FREE TIER NUMBERS - Confirmed by the official pricing page (supabase.com/pricing), which lists for the Free plan: Realtime "Concurrent Peak Connections: 200 included", "Messages Per Month: 2 Million included", and "Max Message Size: 256 KB". (Pro plan for contrast: 500 connections, 5 Million messages/month, 3 MB max.) The official Realtime limits doc (supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime/limits) independently corroborates the 200 concurrent connections and 256 KB payload for Free, though it expresses throughput as "messages per second" (Free = 100/s) rather than a monthly total, so the explicit "2,000,000 messages/month" figure is sourced from the pricing page, not the limits page.

2) INACTIVITY PAUSE - Confirmed by the pricing page: free-tier projects are suspended "after 1 week of inactivity." The claim's "~1 week" is exact. (Note from secondary sources: the timer is keyed to database activity, and data/schema are preserved; the project resumes on next request.)

3) SELF-HOST max_concurrent_users - Confirmed by the official Supabase GitHub discussion #19391, which states self-hosters "can set those limits yourself by setting the max_concurrent_users field on the tenant record."

I attempted to refute but found no contradicting primary evidence. No "uncertain"/"refuted" path applies. Minor caveat: the dedicated self-hosting Realtime config doc URL (docs/guides/self-hosting/realtime/config) currently 404s, so the max_concurrent_users detail rests on the official GitHub discussion rather than that specific doc page.

claim: Ably free = 6M messages/month + 200 concurrent connections + 200 channels; Pusher free Sandbox = 100 connections + 200k messages/day and is non-production only; PubNub free = 200 MAU.
explanation:
All three numeric free-tier figures are confirmed against primary sources as of June 2026, but one qualitative assertion (Pusher being contractually "non-production only") is overstated.

ABLY (CONFIRMED): The official Ably limits page (ably.com/docs/platform/pricing/limits) lists the Free package as exactly 6,000,000 messages/month, 200 concurrent connections (realtime clients connected simultaneously), and 200 concurrent channels (active simultaneously). All three match the claim precisely. Note: the connection/channel limits are CONCURRENT (point-in-time), as the claim implies. The page carries no version/date stamp.

PUSHER (NUMBERS CONFIRMED; "NON-PRODUCTION ONLY" OVERSTATED): The official Pusher Channels pricing page (pusher.com/channels/pricing/) confirms the free Sandbox plan as 100 concurrent connections and 200k messages/day. However, the categorical claim that it "is non-production only" is NOT supported by primary sources. The pricing page, Pusher's "What happens when I hit my limits" docs, and Pusher's own Sandbox-plan blog post (pusher.com/blog/pushers-sandbox-plan/) all describe the Sandbox tier as intended/positioned for development, testing, prototyping, learning, and "small-scale realtime build" — but none of them explicitly prohibit production use or state a contractual non-production restriction. So the Sandbox plan is clearly aimed at non-production/hobby/prototype workloads (which is materially relevant for a PoC — it's fine to use), but "non-production only" overstates what the primary sources actually say.

PUBNUB (CONFIRMED): The official PubNub pricing page (pubnub.com/pricing/) confirms the Free plan includes 200 MAU (Monthly Active Users), and bundles ~1M transactions/function executions and 1GB storage (7-day retention). The 200 MAU figure matches the claim. PubNub bills on MAU, not concurrent connections, which is a meaningfully different metric from Ably/Pusher.

For the PoC decision: Ably's free tier (6M msgs, 200 concurrent conns/channels) is the most generous and explicitly production-usable, making it the strongest managed alternative to Firebase for live multi-user tracking. PubNub's 200 MAU is usable but the unusual MAU-based metric should be modeled against expected unique-user counts. Pusher Sandbox is usable for the PoC but is framed as a development/prototype tier.

claim: The running database is PostgreSQL 18.3 on aarch64 using the plain postgres:latest image with NO PostGIS extension installed; the official postgis/postgis image has PG18 multi-arch (ARM64) tags as of 2025-2026.
explanation:
The first half of the claim is CONFIRMED by direct inspection of the live container; the second half is REFUTED by the Docker Hub registry and the official docs.

CONFIRMED (local environment, verified live on 2026-06-01):
- The db service in /home/ubuntu/.openclaw/workspace/projects/infra/docker-compose.yml uses image: postgres:latest.
- The running postgres-db container reports: "PostgreSQL 18.3 (Debian 18.3-1.pgdg13+1) on aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu" (uname -m = aarch64; host is also aarch64; docker image inspect shows arm64/linux).
- NO PostGIS: pg_extension lists only plpgsql 1.0, and pg_available_extensions returns no postgis* rows. PostGIS is neither installed nor even available in the base image (expected, since the plain postgres image does not bundle it).
- Side note relevant to the migration warning: the PG18 data-directory change is already in effect here -- PGDATA=/var/lib/postgresql/18/docker and the volume mounts /var/lib/postgresql (NOT the legacy /var/lib/postgresql/data). So a future image swap must keep the mount at /var/lib/postgresql to find the existing 18/ data; the existing compose already does this.

REFUTED (the OFFICIAL postgis/postgis image does NOT have PG18 ARM64 tags):
- Docker Hub API for postgis/postgis (name=18) returns exactly 5 PG18 tags: 18-master, 18-3.6, 18-3.6-alpine, 18rc1-3.6, 18rc1-3.6-alpine. Every one of these has only linux/amd64 (plus an unknown/unknown attestation entry). NONE has a linux/arm64 manifest.
- Scanning the repo's tags more broadly: zero tags carry an arm64 image. The official Docker Hub page for postgis/postgis explicitly states "Supported architecture: amd64 (x86-64)" with no mention of ARM64/multi-arch.
- Therefore the official image will NOT run natively on this aarch64 VM; pulling postgis/postgis:18-3.6 would either fail to find a matching manifest or force slow amd64 emulation (qemu).

HOWEVER, an ARM64 PG18 PostGIS image DOES exist via the community fork imresamu/postgis (maintained by Imre Samu, a postgis/docker-postgis contributor). Its PG18 tags are genuinely multi-arch (amd64 + arm64), e.g. 18-3.6, 18-3.6-bookworm, 18-3.6.1-trixie, 18-3.6-alpine3.23, 18-master-bookworm -- all confirmed to publish a linux/arm64 manifest via the Docker Hub API (103 PG18-named tags total). So the underlying GOAL (enable PostGIS on this ARM64 box) is achievable -- just NOT with the official postgis/postgis image as the claim asserts.

IMPLICATION FOR THE RECOMMENDATION: The "swap the image to postgis/postgis:18-x" advice as literally stated is wrong for this aarch64 host. The fix is to pin imresamu/postgis (e.g. imresamu/postgis:18-3.6 or a fully-pinned imresamu/postgis:18-3.6.1-bookworm) instead, OR run PostGIS natively only on an amd64 host. Whichever image is chosen, keep the volume mount at /var/lib/postgresql and back up postgres_data before switching, since the base image change plus any data-dir handling differences can corrupt or orphan the existing 18/ cluster. (Note also the compose mounts the parent /var/lib/postgresql rather than the PGDATA subdir, which is non-standard but works on PG18; verify the replacement image's PGDATA resolves to .../18/docker before starting.)

claim: ST_FrechetDistance was introduced in PostGIS 2.4.0 and requires GEOS >= 3.7.0; ST_LineLocatePoint and ST_DWithin are core stable functions.
explanation:
All three sub-claims are confirmed verbatim by primary PostGIS documentation (postgis.net/docs).

1) ST_FrechetDistance: The official doc page states exactly "Availability: 2.4.0 - requires GEOS >= 3.7.0". Exact match to the claim. (Independently corroborated by the original 2017 commit r15400 adding the function and trac ticket #3677.)

2) ST_LineLocatePoint: Doc states "Availability: 1.1.0" with "Changed: 2.1.0 Up to 2.0.x this was called ST_Line_Locate_Point." It has existed since PostGIS 1.1 (2005-era), is a stable linear-referencing function, has no GEOS-version gate, and is part of the core PostGIS install (no SFCGAL/optional extension needed). "Core stable" is accurate.

3) ST_DWithin: Doc states "Availability: 1.5.0 support for geography was introduced" (the geometry form is even older, predating 1.5). It is a standard OGC Simple Features function, present in every modern PostGIS, and is stable/core. "Core stable" is accurate.

On the version-sensitivity concern (whether the GEOS bundled in a chosen postgis image actually satisfies >= 3.7.0): the official postgis/docker-postgis 16-3.5 Dockerfile pins POSTGIS_VERSION=3.5.2 and pulls libgeos via the Debian/pgdg package manager. PostGIS 3.5 itself requires a far newer GEOS (>= 3.8), so any current 3.5/3.6 image easily clears the 3.7.0 minimum required by ST_FrechetDistance. No refuting evidence found.</explanation>

claim: Self-hosting Valhalla or OSRM map-matching requires building from an OSM extract and can consume several GB of RAM/disk during graph/tile build, competing with Postgres on a constrained Oracle free-tier VM.
explanation:
Primary sources support every element of the claim, with two caveats about magnitude and scope.

1) BUILD-FROM-EXTRACT IS REQUIRED (confirmed). Both engines preprocess an OSM .pbf into their own data structures before serving map-matching: Valhalla via valhalla_build_tiles (produces routing tiles); OSRM via osrm-extract followed by osrm-contract (CH) or osrm-partition+osrm-customize (MLD). This is inherent and documented.

2) "SEVERAL GB OF RAM/DISK DURING BUILD" (confirmed; often an understatement, scales with extract size). Valhalla maintainers state 4GB RAM is "pretty small for building tiles" because the default tile cache is 1GB and with 8 threads totals ~8GB; you must reduce cache size and/or concurrency to build on small RAM. Disk: a Germany PBF (~5GB) yields ~4.6GB of Valhalla tiles, and the build writes many temporary files. OSRM's official wiki (v5.26, Nov-2021 planet data) gives a rule of thumb that runtime RAM roughly equals preprocessing output size (~123GiB for the car planet) and that "sizes scale roughly linear with input data size"; disk during preprocessing is a large multiple of the PBF (a 61GiB planet PBF needs 415GiB disk for car extract). For a small PoC-sized regional extract these figures scale down to the single-digit GB range claimed, but continent/planet builds reach tens-to-hundreds of GB (e.g., a user hit std::bad_alloc running osrm-extract on North America with 32GB RAM).

3) "COMPETING WITH POSTGRES ON A CONSTRAINED ORACLE FREE-TIER VM" (confirmed, directionally). Oracle Always Free ARM (VM.Standard.A1.Flex) tops out at 4 OCPU / 24GB RAM / 200GB shared boot+block storage (or smaller splits; OCI also offers 1GB AMD micro instances). Build-time RAM spikes (tile cache x threads) plus large transient disk usage genuinely contend with a co-resident Postgres + Caddy, especially on a VM sized below the 24GB max. This is the legitimate basis for deferring map-matching in the PoC.

CAVEATS / NUANCE: (a) The heavy multi-GB-to-100GB+ numbers in most sources are for continent/planet builds and should NOT be assumed for a single-metro/small-region PoC extract, where "several GB" is accurate. (b) The cost is primarily a one-time/occasional BUILD cost; once data is built, runtime serving is modest (Valhalla runs in ~4GB; OSRM runtime RAM ~= output size). The Postgres contention is largely avoidable by building artifacts offline/elsewhere and copying them onto the VM, or by lowering cache/concurrency. (c) The 24GB ARM free tier is fairly generous, so "constrained" depends on how the VM was actually sized and provisioned.

claim: Redis sorted sets give O(log N) rank lookups and sub-millisecond top-K reads, but managed Redis free tiers have small/changing limits as of 2026.
explanation:
All parts of the claim are supported by primary sources.

TECHNICAL CLAIMS (Redis official docs, redis.io, retrieved June 2026):
- O(log N) rank lookups: CONFIRMED. ZRANK is documented as "Time complexity: O(log(N))"; ZADD is also O(log(N)) per added element. Sorted sets are backed by a skip list + hash table, which is what gives the logarithmic rank/insert behavior.
- Sub-millisecond top-K reads: CONFIRMED as plausible/accurate. A Strava-style leaderboard top-K is a ZRANGE/ZREVRANGE, documented as O(log(N)+M) where M is the (small) number returned. For top-K (e.g. 10) the M term is negligible, the data is in-memory, and Redis routinely serves such reads in microseconds-to-low-milliseconds. "Sub-millisecond" is an accurate characterization for an in-memory top-K read on a co-located/low-latency Redis (network round-trip to a remote managed instance would dominate, but the operation cost itself is sub-ms).

FREE-TIER CLAIMS ("small/changing limits as of 2026"):
- SMALL: CONFIRMED. Redis Cloud Essentials free plan (docs page last updated Dec 2025): 30 MB dataset, 30 concurrent connections, 100 ops/sec max throughput, 5 GB/month bandwidth, no high availability, community support only. Upstash Redis free tier (pricing docs, June 2026): 256 MB max data, 500K commands/month, 1 database, 10 GB/month bandwidth, 10MB max request size. These are genuinely small for anything beyond prototyping/learning.
- CHANGING: CONFIRMED with dated evidence. Upstash officially changed its free tier on March 12, 2025, moving from "10K commands/day" to "500K commands/month" (Upstash blog), and simultaneously revised Pay-as-You-Go storage (10GB to 100GB) and bandwidth terms. This is concrete proof that managed Redis free-tier limits change. (Notably, Upstash's 2025 change was an INCREASE, not a degradation, but the claim only asserts the limits change frequently, which is true.)

NET: The complexity claims are exact matches to official Redis docs, and the free-tier characterization (small, and subject to change) is backed by current (Dec 2025 / 2025-2026) primary pricing/docs sources plus a dated example of a free-tier change.

claim: MapLibre Native (used by @maplibre/maplibre-react-native, ~v11.2.x in 2026) still has NO 3D terrain / setTerrain support — 3D terrain is web-only (MapLibre GL JS). Only fill-extrusion is available natively.
explanation: Primary sources confirm the claim as of June 2026. (1) MapLibre's official roadmap page for Terrain3D in MapLibre Native (maplibre.org/roadmap/maplibre-native/terrain3d) lists the feature as "Partially funded, please reach out to team@maplibre.org if you are interested in co-sponsoring" — i.e., not implemented or released. (2) GitHub discussion maplibre/maplibre#326 shows it is still a work-in-progress branch (feature/terrain-3d); on 2026-03-19 a contributor said the PR has "a (long) checklist of things that need to be done to finish this feature. I'm not actively working on it at the moment," and on 2026-03-26 the new PR #4190 was opened. (3) PR maplibre/maplibre-native#4190 ("Terrain 3D") is a DRAFT (open, not merged) with most recent activity 2026-04-04; its description lists extensive unfinished work including "3D building support not started," symbol/circle layers rendering at incorrect altitude, line shader behavior, performance concerns, and transparency support pending. So setTerrain-style 3D terrain is NOT available in any native release — it remains effectively web-only (MapLibre GL JS, where setTerrain has shipped since v2/2022). (4) maplibre-react-native release notes (v11.0.0 through latest v11.3.0, 2026-04-17 to 2026-05-30) never mention setTerrain or 3D terrain rendering; the claim's stated ~v11.2.x (v11.2.0 was 2026-05-12) is accurate for the timeframe. NUANCE worth noting for the report: recent maplibre-react-native versions DID add elevation-related primitives — RasterDEMSource and a hillshade layer (v11.1.0) and a color-relief layer (v11.2.0) — but these render 2D shaded-relief visualizations of DEM data, NOT a true 3D terrain mesh / setTerrain. (5) The "only fill-extrusion" part is correct: FillExtrusionLayer (3D extruded polygons/buildings) is fully supported natively and documented at maplibre.org/maplibre-react-native/docs/components/layers/fill-extrusion-layer. Practical implication holds: for a terrain-based 3D replay on an Expo/RN-native map today, you must embed MapLibre GL JS in a WebView.

explanation: Verified by live requests on 2026-06-01 plus primary docs. (1) LIVE + KEYLESS: anonymous credential-free curl to .../terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png returns HTTP 200 image/png (Server: AmazonS3; tiles Last-Modified 2017, a stable archive). No API key/AWS account needed -- the AWS Registry of Open Data page states "No AWS account required," and tilezen/joerd/use-service.md explicitly says the S3 endpoints need no key (unlike the dead Mapzen tile.mapzen.com endpoint, which I confirmed is no longer the access path). (2) CORS: a GET with `Origin: https://example.com` AND a preflight OPTIONS both returned `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET`, `Access-Control-Max-Age: 3000`. This is fully browser/PWA-usable cross-origin -- not just public HTTP. (3) NO PUBLISHED RATE LIMIT: 15 rapid requests all 200, no 429/503; neither the AWS Registry nor joerd docs publish any rate/quota. Caveat: joerd notes the bucket is uncached and "meant for efficient networking with EC2 resources only" -- this is a latency/performance note (recommend fronting with a CDN for production), NOT a throttle or access restriction. (4) MAXZOOM: empirically z13/z14/z15 -> 200, z16 -> 404 NoSuchKey; joerd formats/use-service docs confirm max zoom 15 for the 256px terrarium tiles. The claim's "~13-15" is correct, with 15 the true ceiling. MINOR CAVEAT on the implicit "no attribution requirement": the AWS bucket itself imposes no new throttle/attribution, but the underlying data carries source licenses (joerd/docs/attribution.md). Most coverage (SRTM/GMTED/ETOPO1) is public domain with credit merely *requested*; however some regional sources (NZ LINZ, Norway Kartverket, Australia/Geoscience, EU-DEM, etc.) are CC-BY / open-government and *require* attribution in derived published products. For a PoC demo this is negligible, but a shipped product showing elevation visuals should include standard attribution. Core technical claim (CORS-open, keyless, browser-usable, no published rate limit, maxzoom ~13-15) is CONFIRMED.
