explanation:
Every quantitative component of the claim is confirmed by the official Cesium ion pricing page (cesium.com/platform/cesium-ion/pricing/), fetched 2026-06-01.

1) STREAMING QUOTA: The Community (free) tier provides 15 GB/month streaming quota. CONFIRMED (exact match).

2) STORAGE: The Community tier provides 5 GB storage. CONFIRMED (exact match).

3) NON-COMMERCIAL / LIMITED-EVAL RESTRICTION + ~$50K THRESHOLD: The free Community plan is for "Personal and non-commercial use" plus "Exploratory commercial or government development" for evaluation purposes. A paid account is required if your company "has more than $50K in annual gross revenues or has raised funds in excess of $50K," or for government/funded educational research, or if you surpass usage limits. CONFIRMED. This is the load-bearing risk for the PoC: a public, real product that crosses the $50K revenue-or-funding line, or that is offered commercially to other organizations, must upgrade. (Note: the Community license also does not permit sublicensing/embedding ion in a product made commercially available to other organizations — a separate integration license is required.)

4) NEXT TIER = $149/mo INDIVIDUAL: The next paid tier (Commercial) is $149/month for an individual (and $524/month for a team), with 50 GB storage and 150 GB/month streaming (10x Community). CONFIRMED (exact match for the $149/mo individual figure).

Skeptical cross-check: I attempted to refute via the Cesium Terms of Service page, which does not itself enumerate the $50K threshold (that language lives on the pricing page, which I confirmed). Independent third-party sources (Vendr 2025 pricing, community forum threads) corroborate the $50K revenue/funds-raised threshold, the non-commercial individual framing, and the $149/$524 pricing, so the claim is consistent across primary and secondary sources. No contradicting figures found.

CAVEAT (claimsToVerify): These are time-sensitive pricing/quota numbers. As of 2026-06-01 they match exactly, but Cesium has changed ion pricing/quotas before — re-verify the official pricing page at adoption time. Also confirm whether your specific replay use case counts as 'non-commercial evaluation' vs. a commercial deployment, since that, not just the quota, is what would force an upgrade for a public PoC.

claim: deck.gl TripsLayer requires normalized timestamps (not raw Unix epoch) due to 32-bit float precision, and interleaved compositing with MapLibre requires WebGL2 / maplibre-gl >= 3.
explanation:
Both halves of the claim are verified verbatim against the deck.gl official documentation (visgl/deck.gl repo, master branch), the authoritative primary source.

PART 1 - Timestamp normalization / 32-bit float precision: The TripsLayer API reference states explicitly: "Because timestamps are stored as 32-bit floating numbers, raw unix epoch time can not be used." It further advises: "You may test the validity of a timestamp by calling Math.fround(t) to check if there would be any loss of precision." The documented and example-driven remedy is to normalize timestamps by subtracting a fixed baseline (start time) so the values fall within the ~2^24 (~190 days at 1s resolution) range a float32 can represent without loss. This directly corroborates the claim and the stated failure mode (passing raw epoch yields incorrect/garbled animation because the timestamps lose precision and effectively collapse). CONFIRMED.

PART 2 - Interleaved compositing requires WebGL2 / maplibre-gl >= 3: The deck.gl "Using with MapLibre" developer guide states, in the Interleaved integration-mode section (which is what enables true compositing such as deck.gl layers under MapLibre labels and correct 3D depth occlusion), verbatim: "It requires WebGL2 and therefore only works with maplibre-gl@>3." Interleaving is achieved via MapboxOverlay with interleaved: true from @deck.gl/mapbox. CONFIRMED. (Note: the non-interleaved/overlaid mode does NOT require WebGL2; the WebGL2 + maplibre-gl>=3 requirement is specific to the interleaved mode, which is exactly what the claim references for "interleaved compositing.")

The framing of why it matters is also accurate: epoch-timestamp precision loss is a well-known gotcha (see also visgl/deck.gl issues) and interleaved mode is the mode needed for proper layer ordering/3D occlusion in a Strava-style 3D replay.

TIME/VERSION SENSITIVITY: Evidence is from the deck.gl docs master branch fetched 2026-06-01. The maplibre-gl>=3 requirement is version-pinned and could shift in future major releases; current MapLibre GL JS is well past v3 (v3 introduced WebGL2/globe in May 2023), so the requirement is comfortably satisfied by any current MapLibre version. The float32 timestamp constraint is a structural limitation of the layer's attribute encoding and is stable across recent versions (also present in the 8.7-release docs), but should be re-checked if a future deck.gl release changes timestamp attribute precision (e.g., to float64 via the Fp64 / double-precision path).

claim: Firebase Auth free tier = 50,000 MAU/month with email + social free, but phone/SMS auth is metered (~$0.01-$0.06/SMS) and requires the Blaze plan. Verified against firebase.google.com/pricing as of June 2026.
explanation:
The load-bearing parts of the claim are confirmed by primary Firebase/Google sources, with one numerical caveat on the SMS rate ceiling.

CONFIRMED by primary sources:
- 50,000 MAU free tier: firebase.google.com/pricing states the free Spark plan includes "50K MAUs" at no cost; the Blaze (pay-as-you-go) plan keeps the same 50K free allowance for standard auth.
- Email + social free: the official pricing table shows standard auth methods (email/password, anonymous, social logins) are included free within the MAU limit on both Spark and Blaze.
- Phone/SMS auth is metered: firebase.google.com/pricing lists Phone Auth as "Billed per SMS sent" (rates vary by region), and the dedicated Phone Number Verification pricing page confirms per-verification billing.
- Requires Blaze plan: STRONGLY confirmed by two official docs. firebase.google.com/docs/auth/limits states verbatim "Verification code SMS messages: Pay as you go (Blaze) plan only." firebase.google.com/docs/projects/billing/firebase-pricing-plans lists "Authentication (phone)" as a paid-tier product requiring an active Cloud Billing account (Blaze). So the PoC's "fully free" assumption does break if phone login is needed — the claim's "why it matters" reasoning holds.

CAVEAT (why partly-true, not confirmed):
- The "~$0.01-$0.06/SMS" range is directionally right at the low end (commonly cited $0.01 for US/Canada/India, ~$0.06 rest-of-world) but UNDERSTATES the high end. Firebase's newer dedicated Phone Number Verification pricing page (firebase.google.com/docs/phone-number-verification/pricing, last updated 2026-05-27) lists per-verification rates that exceed $0.06 for several countries — e.g., Germany ~$0.0810-$0.0875, Indonesia ~$0.125-$0.135, Pakistan ~$0.100-$0.108. Secondary sources also note premium carriers up to ~$0.34. So per-verification cost can be 2-5x the claimed ceiling depending on region.
- The exact $0.01/$0.06 figures could not be read directly off the cloud.google.com/identity-platform/pricing page (page content was truncated on fetch); they are supported by secondary sources (metacto, rapidnative) and the official pricing page's "varies by region / billed per SMS sent" language, but the precise tier table was not independently confirmed from the primary Google source in this check.
- Minor: a free monthly verification allowance (secondary sources cite ~10,000/month on the newer product) may exist before paid pricing kicks in — not mentioned in the claim, but doesn't contradict it.

Net: the claim's qualitative structure (50K MAU free, email/social free, phone/SMS metered and Blaze-only) is accurate per primary docs; only the upper bound of the SMS price range is too low for non-US/EU-core regions.

claim: FCM is free and unlimited on both Spark and Blaze, but the legacy FCM server-key API was shut down July 2024 — the NestJS server must use the FCM HTTP v1 API with a Google service-account JSON.
explanation:
All four sub-claims hold against primary sources, with one minor date nuance worth flagging.

1) FCM free/unlimited on both plans — CONFIRMED. The official Firebase pricing page (firebase.google.com/pricing) lists Cloud Messaging as "No-cost" identically under both the Spark (no-cost) and Blaze (pay-as-you-go) plans, with no usage limit or quota stated. FCM message sending itself carries no per-message charge on either plan. (Caveat to flag: "unlimited" is true for FCM message dispatch, but if you trigger FCM via Cloud Functions or store device tokens in Firestore, those adjacent services have their own quotas/billing — FCM-the-messaging-service is free, the surrounding plumbing may not be.)

2) Legacy server-key API shut down — CONFIRMED. The legacy FCM APIs (legacy HTTP protocol and XMPP, which authenticated with a static "Server key") were deprecated on June 20, 2023, and Google shut them down in 2024. Authentication moved from the static server key to Google service accounts.

3) "July 2024" date — SUBSTANTIALLY CORRECT, with a common-confusion caveat. The actual shutdown began July 22, 2024 (per Firebase's migrate-v1 guidance: "deprecated on June 20, 2023, and shutdown begins on July 22, 2024"). Google had originally announced June 20, 2024 as the cutoff and later pushed it to July 22, 2024, which is why many secondary sources (including the react-native-firebase discussion and several vendor guides) still cite "June 20, 2024." The claim's "July 2024" matches the final official shutdown month, so it is correct — but be aware of the widespread June-20 references when reading older tutorials.

4) NestJS must use HTTP v1 with service-account JSON — CONFIRMED. The FCM HTTP v1 API authenticates with OAuth 2.0 Bearer access tokens minted from a Google service account (scope https://www.googleapis.com/auth/firebase.messaging). On a non-Google server like a self-hosted NestJS app on the Oracle VM, that means supplying a service-account JSON private key (or Application Default Credentials). In practice you'd use the firebase-admin SDK (admin.messaging()), which handles token minting from the service-account credentials. The "why it matters" warning is accurate: any code hitting the old fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send endpoint with an Authorization: key=<SERVER_KEY> header will now fail — endpoints moved to fcm.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{project}/messages:send with a Bearer token.

Verdict: confirmed. The only nuance is the June-20 vs July-22 2024 date confusion, but the claim's "July 2024" is the correct final shutdown month.

claim: MinIO's GitHub repository was archived (~Feb 2026) and official MinIO Docker images were discontinued (~Oct 2025), pushing self-hosters to Bitnami/community images.
explanation:
The core thrust of the claim is CONFIRMED by primary sources, but two details are imprecise — most importantly the "Bitnami" fallback.

1) DOCKER IMAGES DISCONTINUED (~Oct 2025): CONFIRMED. MinIO stopped publishing official Docker images to Docker Hub and Quay.io on/around 15 Oct 2025, coinciding with a security release. Primary evidence: GitHub issue minio/minio#21647 — a user asking why the 2025-10-15 security release has no image on Docker Hub/Quay.io — is labeled "community" and "working as intended" by maintainers, i.e. the absence is deliberate. The minio/minio Docker Hub repo's latest tag is RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z (no newer pushes). MinIO's position is now "source-only distribution; build your own container images." The "~Oct 2025" date is accurate.

2) GITHUB REPO ARCHIVED (~Feb 2026): MOSTLY CONFIRMED, date slightly imprecise. The live github.com/minio/minio banner now reads "THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED" and "This repository was archived by the owner on Apr 25, 2026. It is now read-only." The "NO LONGER MAINTAINED" status text reportedly appeared ~14 Feb 2026 (after a 3 Dec 2025 "maintenance mode" announcement), but the FORMAL read-only archival was 25 Apr 2026, not February. So "archived ~Feb 2026" conflates the status change (~Feb) with the actual archive flag (~Apr). The README now steers users to AIStor Free/Enterprise.

3) "PUSHING SELF-HOSTERS TO BITNAMI/COMMUNITY IMAGES": PARTLY WRONG on Bitnami. Because upstream stopped publishing releases, the free bitnami/minio image ALSO stopped — hub.docker.com/r/bitnami/minio now states the image "is no longer available for free through Docker Hub" and is offered only via a commercial Bitnami Secure Images subscription (this is also tied to Broadcom's broader 2025 Bitnami free-tier wind-down). So Bitnami is NOT a viable free fallback. Self-hosters were instead pushed to COMMUNITY rebuilds — coollabsio/minio, golithus/minio-builds, and the pgsty/minio fork (which restores the console and rebuilds binaries under the irrevocable AGPL license).

NET: The decision-relevant conclusion for the PoC holds and is arguably STRENGTHENED — official MinIO is now unmaintained/archived and ships no official containers, and even Bitnami is no longer a free option, leaving only community-maintained forks. This is a strong reason to prefer Cloudflare R2 over self-hosted MinIO for a new PoC. The claim is rated partly-true only because (a) formal archival was Apr 2026 not Feb, and (b) Bitnami is no longer free, so "Bitnami/community" overstates Bitnami's availability.

CLAIMS TO VERIFY / TIME-SENSITIVE: archive date (Apr 25 2026 per live repo) vs status-change date (~Feb 14 2026); whether any community fork (pgsty/minio, coollabsio/minio) becomes a de-facto maintained successor; current free-tier status of Bitnami Secure Images (Broadcom policy changing through 2025-2026); and Cloudflare R2 free-tier limits (10 GB storage, no egress fees as of 2026) should be reconfirmed before relying on them.

claim: Supabase free projects PAUSE after 7 days of inactivity and the free plan allows only 2 active projects, with 500 MB DB / 1 GB file storage / 50K MAU.
explanation:
Every element of the claim is confirmed by Supabase's own primary sources as of 2026-06-01.

PAUSE AFTER 7 DAYS: The official pricing page states "Free projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity." The official going-into-prod docs state "We may pause applications on the Free Plan that exhibit low activity in a 7-day period to save on server resources." 1 week = 7 days, so the "7 days" figure is accurate. Note a nuance worth flagging: the trigger is database INACTIVITY (no queries reaching the DB), not merely "no demo." A resumed project takes ~30s to wake. This is a genuine UX hazard for a sporadically-demoed PoC, exactly as the claim's rationale states. Pausing can be avoided via a periodic ping/cron (community workarounds exist) or by upgrading to Pro ($25/mo/project), which removes the pause.

2 ACTIVE PROJECTS: Pricing page states "Limit of 2 active projects." Billing docs add nuance: "Paused projects do not count towards your free project limit," and "two free projects... two Free Plan organizations with one project each, or one Free Plan organization with two projects." So the active-project ceiling is exactly 2, confirming the claim.

500 MB DB: Confirmed verbatim — "500 MB database size (Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM)."

1 GB FILE STORAGE: Confirmed verbatim — "1 GB file storage."

50K MAU: Confirmed verbatim — "50,000 monthly active users." (MAU counts only users who authenticate within a calendar month, not total registered users.)

For comparison context relevant to the recommendation: Firebase Auth's Spark (free) plan has no project-inactivity pause, which is why it is a safer choice for an intermittently-demoed PoC on this dimension.

claim: Open-Meteo's free Elevation API is NON-COMMERCIAL only, uses Copernicus GLO-90 (90m), allows up to 100 coordinates per request, and is rate-limited to ~10,000 calls/day (5,000/hour, 600/minute) as of 2026.
explanation:
Every element of the claim is supported by Open-Meteo primary sources, with no refuting evidence found.

1) DEM dataset / resolution — CONFIRMED. The official Elevation API docs (open-meteo.com/en/docs/elevation-api) state the data is based on the "Copernicus DEM 2021 release GLO-90" at "90 meters resolution," available worldwide under a free licence. Exactly matches "Copernicus GLO-90 (90m)."

2) Up to 100 coordinates per request — CONFIRMED. The docs explicitly state "Up to 100 coordinates can be requested at once." Exactly matches the claim.

3) Non-commercial only — CONFIRMED. The Terms page (open-meteo.com/en/terms) states the free API may only be used for non-commercial purposes, with non-commercial use "defined as elaborated by creative commons" (CC-BY 4.0), and lists commercial use (subscriptions, advertising, integration into commercial products, for-profit research) as requiring a paid/commercial licence. The pricing page confirms the Free tier is "non-commercial use only." This validates the claim's "why it matters" concern: turning the PoC into a product would require leaving the free hosted path.

4) Rate limits — CONFIRMED. The Terms page states the free API is limited to "Less than 10,000 API calls per day, 5,000 per hour and 600 per minute." The pricing page repeats "600 calls / min, 5,000 calls / hour, 10,000 calls / day." The Open-Meteo creator independently confirmed the same figures on Hacker News (comment ~4 months prior to June 2026): "The limits are 600 calls / min, 5.000 calls / hour and 10.000 calls / day," enforced per IP address. The claim's "~10,000/day" approximation correctly reflects the official "less than 10,000" phrasing.

claim: Google Maps Elevation API now offers only 5,000 free calls/month (the $200/mo credit ended Feb 28 2025) and then charges $5.00 per 1,000 requests.
explanation:
Every element of the claim is confirmed by Google's own primary documentation as of June 2026.

1) $200 credit ended Feb 28, 2025: Google's official Elevation API usage-and-billing page states verbatim that the Elevation API "utilizes a pay-as-you-go pricing model... with a $200 monthly credit available until February 28, 2025." Google's "March 2025 changes" billing docs confirm the unified, cross-API $200 monthly recurring credit was retired and replaced (effective March 1, 2025) with per-SKU free monthly usage caps that no longer pool across APIs.

2) 5,000 free calls/month: Google's core-services pricing list classifies the Elevation API (SKU B43B-2A59-C153) under the "Pro" tier, and Pro SKUs receive 5,000 free calls per SKU per month (Essentials get 10,000; Enterprise get 1,000). So Elevation specifically gets 5,000 free calls/month.

3) $5.00 per 1,000 requests: The pricing list shows Elevation's lowest/entry tier at $5.00 CPM (per 1,000) for usage between the 5,000 free cap and 100,000 monthly events. (Volume discounts apply above that: ~$4.00 per 1,000 at 100,001-500,000, declining to ~$0.38 per 1,000 at 5,000,000+ events — but the headline rate after the free cap is indeed $5.00/1,000.)

Implication for the report: This rules Google out as a meaningfully "free" elevation source for anything beyond trivial usage. A single user generating elevation profiles for routes can easily exceed 5,000 calls/month (each elevation request typically samples many points, and a busy app makes many requests), so the cost-effective path for elevation profiles, gain/loss, and 3D terrain is self-hosting open DEM data (e.g., Copernicus DEM GLO-30, SRTM) and querying it locally.

Minor nuance worth noting for precision: the claim's phrasing "offers only 5,000 free calls/month" is accurate for the Elevation API SKU, but be aware the new model is per-SKU, so other APIs (Essentials) get 10,000 free — the 5,000 figure is specific to Pro-tier services like Elevation. Also, prices are USD on the standard (non-India) pricing list.

claim: AWS Mapzen Terrarium terrain tiles (s3://elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png) and the Copernicus DEM buckets (copernicus-dem-30m / -90m, COGs) are free and open with no AWS account required, and Terrarium decodes as elevation_m = (R*256 + G + B/256) - 32768.
explanation:
All three sub-claims are supported by primary sources and live tests.

1) TERRARIUM BUCKET + PATH (confirmed): The AWS Registry of Open Data lists the dataset as arn:aws:s3:::elevation-tiles-prod (us-east-1), managed by "Mapzen, a Linux Foundation project", with an EU replica arn:aws:s3:::elevation-tiles-prod-eu (eu-central-1). The official tilezen/joerd use-service docs give the public S3 endpoint https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png and explicitly state it does NOT require an API key (unlike the retired tile.mapzen.com endpoint). LIVE TEST: GET https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/10/300/400.png returned HTTP 200 with a valid 113806-byte image/png, with NO AWS credentials. The bucket-virtual-host form https://elevation-tiles-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/terrarium/0/0/0.png also returned HTTP 200. So "free, no account required" is confirmed in practice.

2) DECODE FORMULA (confirmed verbatim): The official tilezen/joerd docs/formats.md states the Terrarium decode as exactly "(red * 256 + green + blue / 256) - 32768", identical to the claim. Format: PNG, 24-bit fixed point, 32768 m offset, 16 bits integer + 8 bits fraction across R/G/B channels.

3) COPERNICUS DEM BUCKETS (confirmed): The AWS Registry of Open Data (registry.opendata.aws/copernicus-dem) lists arn:aws:s3:::copernicus-dem-30m (GLO-30 Public) and arn:aws:s3:::copernicus-dem-90m (GLO-90), both eu-central-1, provided as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, free for the general public under the Copernicus license, with explicit "(No AWS account required)" and aws s3 ls --no-sign-request examples. LIVE TEST: unauthenticated HTTPS list of copernicus-dem-30m returned HTTP 200 with COG object keys (e.g., Copernicus_DSM_COG_10_N00_00_E006_00_DEM/...).

NUANCES (do not refute the claim): (a) The claim writes the source as the s3:// URI; for a browser/PWA you must use the HTTPS form (https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/... or https://elevation-tiles-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/...) — both confirmed working with CORS-less direct GETs returning 200. (b) joerd docs note the raw S3 endpoint is "meant for efficient networking with EC2 resources only" and serves 256px terrarium tiles — this is guidance/etiquette, not an access restriction. (c) For the COGs, decoding is via GDAL/rio-tiler (raw float meters), NOT the Terrarium RGB formula — the claim correctly scopes the formula to Terrarium only.
